title: Why do so many lifters quit once they become intermediates?
summary: NH asks why, given millions of people consuming YouTube fitness, there are so few elite naturals, and argues most lifters quit or stagnate at the intermediate stage. Reasons: they are content once they look good or are strong enough, progress stops being easy, novice programs rush them into a plateau they cannot navigate, and they lack a long-term goal. He describes the YouTube fitness audience as a recycled pool of newcomers.

claims.claim: Most lifters quit or stagnate permanently once they reach the intermediate stage, which is why there are so few elite natural physiques and strength levels despite millions following YouTube fitness.
Insane physiques and insane strength can both be achieved more or less naturally; it mainly takes time, which is exactly where people fall off.
Many people quit because they are satisfied: once they reach what they consider acceptable looks or strength they stop, and there is nothing wrong with that.
An attractive physique, or being stronger than 95% of the population, does not take many years of hard work, and once achieved it is easy to maintain.
Others quit when lifting stops being easy: past a certain point you have to invest much more work to get much less back, which discourages many naturals.

He believes 99% of people who talk about having reached their natural limit never actually reached it; the real limit is much further than people think. What they reached is the point where the investment no longer seems worth it.

Many novice programs fast-track lifters through the novice stage with rapid linear strength progress, which is designed to end in a set of five they cannot hit; after repeated failures they plateau and lose all momentum.

Novices who only ever followed a program never learn how to program, so when they plateau they either luckily find a better program or quit, often restarting years later as novices and repeating the cycle.
Far more people have a 400 lb deadlift than a 500 lb deadlift, and the gap is not just genetics and strength potential but the amount of work people are willing to put in.

Having a long-term goal is the most important thing; the novice phase should open windows onto what you want to pursue next (aesthetics, strength, athletic prowess), not just a number like a 45-inch chest.
Novice programs can turn followers into progress-obsessed drones who never ask what the progress is for.
His definition of an intermediate: someone who can answer the question 'why do you lift?'
The YouTube fitness audience is largely recycled: maybe 10-15% are in it for the long run, while the majority is constantly renewed by newcomers who drive views on mainstream channels.
Newcomers are the future of the sport and should be taught well; the goal of experienced lifters should be to help them stay in the game long-term rather than dropping out after one or two years.
